los.text: Describe the anatomical features of the male external genitalia
los.html:
Penis
  • Root (fixed in the superficial perineal pouch: two crura + bulb), body (shaft: two corpora cavernosa + corpus spongiosum), glans (expanded end of the corpus spongiosum) with the external urethral meatus
  • Corona, prepuce (foreskin), frenulum.
ScrotumSkin pouch holding the testes, divided by a septum; dartos muscle.
Supporting ligamentsFundiform and suspensory ligaments of the penis.

los.text: Identify the components of the male internal genital organs, recall their functions and anatomical relationships, and predict sites of referred pain from pelvic viscera
los.html:
OrganFunctionRelations
TestisSperm and testosteroneIn the scrotum; descended from the posterior abdominal wall
EpididymisStores and matures spermAlong the back of the testis (head, body, tail)
Vas deferensCarries sperm to the ejaculatory ductSpermatic cord → deep ring → crosses over the ureter → behind the bladder (ampulla)
Seminal vesicles~70% of semen volume (fructose, prostaglandins)Behind the bladder, in front of the rectum, lateral to the vas ampullae
Ejaculatory ductsVas + seminal vesicle ductThrough the prostate → seminal colliculus (prostatic urethra)
Prostate~30% of semen (PSA, zinc, citrate)Below the bladder, in front of the rectum (felt on DRE), on the pelvic floor
Bulbourethral glandsPre-ejaculate mucusDeep perineal pouch
Referred pain fromFelt inWhy
TestisPeriumbilical / T10 region and loinTestis develops at T10 level, its nerves come with the testicular artery
Ureter (stone)Loin to groin, scrotumT11–L2 and genitofemoral nerve
Prostate, seminal vesiclesPerineum, lower back, rectumS2–4, T11–L2
BladderSuprapubic area (fundus), perineum and penis tip (neck)

los.text: Label a cross-sectional diagram of the penis taken at any level
los.html:
• Cross-section of the body of the penis (dorsal surface at the top):
PositionStructure
Dorsal midline (outside Buck's fascia)Superficial dorsal vein
Dorsal midline (inside Buck's fascia)Deep dorsal vein (midline), dorsal arteries (either side), dorsal nerves (most lateral)
Paired, dorsalCorpora cavernosa, each with a deep (cavernosal) artery in the centre, wrapped in tunica albuginea
Single, ventralCorpus spongiosum containing the spongy urethra
Around all threeDeep (Buck's) fascia
OutsideSuperficial (dartos) fascia, skin
  • Root (perineum): crura (covered by ischiocavernosus) attached to the ischiopubic rami
    • bulb (covered by bulbospongiosus) on the perineal membrane, with the urethra entering it from above.

los.text: Identify the dorsal surface of the penis
los.html:
Dorsal surface
  • The surface that faces forwards/upwards when flaccid (the opposite side from the urethra).
  • It carries the deep dorsal vein, dorsal arteries and dorsal nerves.
Why "dorsal"in the erect (anatomical) position the penis points up, so this surface is the back.
Ventral (urethral) surfaceThe corpus spongiosum and urethra; the frenulum is on this side.

los.text: Describe the innervation, arterial supply, venous and lymphatic drainage of the penis
los.html:
SupplyDetail
ArteriesInternal pudendal artery → dorsal artery (skin, glans), deep artery (corpora cavernosa: helicine arteries → erection), artery of the bulb (spongiosum)
Veins
  • Deep dorsal vein → under the pubic symphysis → prostatic venous plexus
  • Superficial dorsal vein → external pudendal → great saphenous
LymphSkin of penis → superficial inguinal nodes; glans and erectile tissue → deep inguinal and internal iliac nodes
Nerves
  • Sensory: dorsal nerve of the penis (pudendal, S2–4)
  • Ilioinguinal to the root.
  • Autonomic: cavernous nerves (parasympathetic S2–4: erection; sympathetic T11–L2: emission and detumescence) from the prostatic plexus

los.text: Explain the anatomy of the perineal membrane and superficial perineal pouch in relation to the accumulation of fluids in the male
los.html:
Perineal membraneStrong fascial sheet across the urogenital triangle between the ischiopubic rami; separates the deep and superficial pouches.
Superficial perineal pouch
  • Between the perineal membrane and the membranous layer of superficial fascia (Colles').
  • Contains the root of the penis, ischiocavernosus, bulbospongiosus, superficial transverse perineal muscles.
Colles' fascia attachments
  • Fused to the perineal membrane behind and the fascia lata below the inguinal ligament at the sides
  • Continuous with dartos (scrotum, penis) and Scarpa's fascia of the abdominal wall.
InjuryWhat happens
Rupture of the spongy urethra (straddle injury on the bulb)
  • Urine extravasates into the superficial pouch → spreads into the scrotum, penis and up the anterior abdominal wall (under Scarpa's fascia)
  • Not into the thighs (attachment to fascia lata) or the anal triangle (attachment to perineal membrane)
Membranous urethra rupture (pelvic fracture)Urine collects in the deep pouch and extraperitoneal pelvis
  • Clinical: blood at the meatus after trauma → don't catheterise (retrograde urethrogram first).

los.text: Identify the scrotum and describe its structure, attachments, innervation, arterial supply, venous and lymphatic drainage
los.html:
Layers(out → in)
  • Skin
  • Dartos (smooth muscle, wrinkles skin in cold)
  • External spermatic fascia
  • Cremaster muscle and fascia
  • Internal spermatic fascia
  • Tunica vaginalis (parietal and visceral).
AttachmentsContinuous with the perineum; septum divides it; gubernaculum remnant (scrotal ligament) tethers the testis to the scrotal floor.
SupplyDetail
ArteriesExternal pudendal (femoral) in front; posterior scrotal (internal pudendal) behind; cremasteric artery
VeinsFollow the arteries → great saphenous and internal pudendal veins
LymphSuperficial inguinal nodes (not the testis's para-aortic nodes)
NervesFront: ilioinguinal (L1) and genital branch of genitofemoral (L1–2); back: posterior scrotal (pudendal, S3) and posterior femoral cutaneous (S2)
  • Temperature: dartos and cremaster pull the testes up in the cold
    • the pampiniform plexus cools arterial blood (counter-current) to ~2–3 °C below core.

los.text: Identify structures within the spermatic cord
los.html:
Contents of the spermatic cordDetail
Vas deferensFirm, cord-like, felt at the back of the cord
Testicular arteryFrom the aorta (L2)
Pampiniform plexusBecomes the testicular vein
Artery to the vasInferior vesical artery
Cremasteric arteryInferior epigastric
Genital branch of genitofemoral nerveCremaster muscle (cremasteric reflex)
Autonomic nervesSympathetic (T10)
LymphaticsTo para-aortic nodes
Processus vaginalis remnantPatent → indirect hernia, hydrocele
Coverings(from the abdominal wall layers)External spermatic fascia (external oblique), cremasteric fascia and muscle (internal oblique), internal spermatic fascia (transversalis fascia).
Ilioinguinal nerveRuns outside the cord in the inguinal canal.

los.text: Explain the structure of the tunica vaginalis testis
los.html:
Tunica vaginalisClosed serous sac from the processus vaginalis (peritoneum carried down with the testis), which normally closes above.
LayersVisceral (on the front and sides of the testis and epididymis) and parietal (lining the scrotal layers), with a potential space between.
AbnormalityCause
HydroceleFluid in the tunica vaginalis; transilluminates; can get above it
Communicating hydrocele / indirect inguinal herniaProcessus vaginalis stays open
Bell-clapper deformityTunica vaginalis surrounds the whole testis, so it can twist → torsion
HaematoceleBlood after trauma

los.text: Describe the structure of the testis, epididymis and their coverings
los.html:
StructureDetail
CoveringsTunica vaginalis (outside), tunica albuginea (tough capsule), tunica vasculosa
TestisSepta divide it into ~250 lobules; each holds seminiferous tubules (sperm; Sertoli cells) with Leydig cells between (testosterone)
DuctsTubules → rete testis (mediastinum) → efferent ductules → epididymis
Epididymis
  • Head (on top, receives efferent ductules), body, tail → vas deferens
  • a single coiled duct ~6 m long
  • Sperm mature and gain motility over ~12 days
  • Appendix testis (paramesonephric remnant): can twist (blue dot sign), mimicking torsion.

los.text: Describe the autonomic nervous, arterial supply, venous and lymph drainage of the testis and epididymis
los.html:
SupplyTestis and epididymis
ArteriesTesticular artery (aorta, L2); artery to the vas; cremasteric artery
VeinsPampiniform plexus → testicular vein: right → IVC, left → left renal vein
LymphPara-aortic (lumbar) nodes at L1–2
Autonomic nerves
  • Sympathetic from T10 (via the renal and aortic plexuses along the testicular artery)
  • Visceral afferents → pain referred to the periumbilical region

los.text: Explain the significance of the arterial supply of the testis in relation to torsion, the venous drainage in relation to varicocoele and the lymphatic drainage in relation to tumour spread
los.html:
FeatureSignificance
Arterial supply: one main testicular artery, an end artery in effect
  • Torsion twists the cord and cuts off the supply → infarction within ~6 hours.
  • Sudden severe pain, high-riding horizontal testis, lost cremasteric reflex.
  • Emergency surgery: untwist and fix both testes
Venous drainage: left testicular vein enters the left renal vein at a right angle; longer; no/fewer valves
  • Varicocele (bag of worms) usually left-sided
  • a new left varicocele in an older man can signal a left renal tumour blocking the renal vein
Lymph: to para-aortic nodes (testis descended from there)Testicular cancer spreads to para-aortic nodes first (not inguinal); so never biopsy through the scrotum (inguinal orchidectomy)
Scrotal skin lymph → inguinal nodesScrotal skin cancers spread to inguinal nodes

los.text: Describe the structure and function of the prostate
los.html:
• Prostate: fibromuscular gland around the prostatic urethra, below the bladder neck
    • walnut-sized (~20 g)
    • base above, apex below on the pelvic floor.
Zone% of glandDisease
Peripheral~70% (back and sides)Cancer (~70%); felt on DRE
Transition~5% (around the urethra)BPH
Central~25% (around the ejaculatory ducts)
Anterior fibromuscular stromaNon-glandular
FunctionSecretes ~30% of semen (PSA liquefies semen, zinc, citrate); smooth muscle helps expel semen; contributes to continence (bladder neck).
Relations
  • Front = pubic symphysis (retropubic space, prostatic venous plexus)
  • Back = rectum (separated by Denonvilliers' fascia)
  • Below = external sphincter, pelvic floor
  • Above = bladder neck, seminal vesicles.
Blood
  • Inferior vesical artery
  • Prostatic venous plexus → internal iliac veins and the vertebral venous plexus (Batson's) → spread of cancer to the spine.
  • Lymph: internal iliac nodes.

los.text: Describe the normal form of the prostate when examined per rectum and changes in relation to hypertrophy and malignancy
los.html:
NormalBPHCancer
SizeWalnut, ~3–4 cmEnlargedNormal or enlarged
SurfaceSmoothSmoothHard, irregular, craggy nodule(s)
ConsistencyRubbery, firmRubberyHard
Median sulcusPalpable between two lateral lobesOften still felt (may be lost)Lost/obliterated in advanced disease
EdgesDistinctDistinctIndistinct, fixed
Rectal mucosaMoves freely over itMoves freelyMay be fixed
  • DRE: patient on left side, knees up; feel through the anterior rectal wall.

los.text: Describe the innervation and mechanisms involved in erection of cavernous tissue and emission and ejaculation
los.html:
StageNervesMechanism
ErectionParasympathetic pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–4) → cavernous nerves
  • NO
  • → cGMP
  • → smooth muscle of helicine arteries and sinusoids relaxes
  • → blood fills the corpora cavernosa
  • → veins compressed against the tunica albuginea (venous occlusion)
  • Ischiocavernosus and bulbospongiosus (pudendal) increase rigidity
EmissionSympathetic (T11–L2)
  • Smooth muscle of the epididymis, vas, seminal vesicles and prostate contracts → semen into the prostatic urethra
  • Bladder neck closes (no retrograde ejaculation)
EjaculationSomatic: pudendal (S2–4) + sympatheticRhythmic contraction of bulbospongiosus expels semen from the urethra
DetumescenceSympatheticArteries constrict, veins drain
"Point and shoot"Parasympathetic points, Sympathetic shoots (emission), Somatic squirts.
Clinical
  • PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil) keep cGMP high
  • Radical prostatectomy and rectal surgery can damage the cavernous nerves
  • α-blockers can cause retrograde ejaculation.

los.text: Trace the path of sperm and fluids through the male reproductive tracts
los.html:
1Seminiferous tubules (sperm produced).
2. Rete testisEfferent ductules.
3. Epididymis(head → body → tail)Storage and maturation.
4. Vas deferens
  • Up the spermatic cord
  • → superficial ring
  • → inguinal canal
  • → deep ring
  • → over the external iliac vessels
  • → down the pelvic side wall
  • → crosses over the ureter
  • → ampulla behind the bladder.
5Ejaculatory duct (vas + seminal vesicle duct) through the prostate.
6. Prostatic urethra(prostatic secretions added)Membranous urethra → spongy urethra (bulbourethral gland secretions) → external urethral meatus.
FluidsSeminal vesicles ~70% (fructose), prostate ~30% (PSA), bulbourethral glands (pre-ejaculate), sperm <5%.
Mnemonic(path)SEVEN UP: Seminiferous tubules, Epididymis, Vas deferens, Ejaculatory duct, (Nothing), Urethra, Penis.

los.text: Describe the path of the male urethra and recognise its three parts (prostatic, membranous and spongy), and the position of the external urethral sphincter
los.html:
PartLengthFeatures
Preprostatic (bladder neck)~1 cmInternal urethral sphincter (smooth, sympathetic): prevents retrograde ejaculation
Prostatic~3–4 cmWidest, most dilatable; seminal colliculus with ejaculatory duct openings and prostatic utricle; prostatic ducts
Membranous~1–2 cm
  • Shortest, narrowest, least dilatable
  • Passes through the deep perineal pouch, surrounded by the external urethral sphincter (voluntary, pudendal)
  • Torn in pelvic fractures
Spongy (penile)~15 cmLongest; in the corpus spongiosum; bulbourethral gland ducts open into its proximal part; navicular fossa in the glans
  • Total ~18–22 cm; two curves (fixed at the bulb, mobile in the flaccid penis).
  • External urethral sphincter: in the deep perineal pouch, around the membranous urethra.

los.text: Explain the functions of the bulbourethral glands
los.html:
Bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands
  • Pea-sized pair in the deep perineal pouch, beside the membranous urethra
  • Ducts pierce the perineal membrane to open into the proximal spongy urethra.
FunctionSecrete clear mucus (pre-ejaculate) during arousal that lubricates the urethra and neutralises acidic urine residue before ejaculation, protecting sperm.
Female homologueGreater vestibular (Bartholin's) glands.
